newsitem.title: GERMANY: Budget deficit stokes German coalition row.
newsitem.headline: Budget deficit stokes German coalition row.

text.p: Germany's centrist Free Democrats (FDP), junior members of Helmut Kohl's coalition, turned up the heat at the weekend in an increasingly bitter row with their conservative partners over how to plug new gaps in the budget.

The FDP is struggling to maintain credibility as the party of tax cuts after being forced this month to wave goodbye to an income tax cut it appeared to have secured earlier this year. It is now desperate at least to prevent taxes being raised.
"Our coalition partners know that the FDP will not agree to tax increases," party leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told the news weekly Der Spiegel.
Asked if this meant a rise in tax would mean the end of the coalition, Gerhardt replied: "You can put it that way. But there will be no tax increases, and so the coalition will not end."
The weekly Welt am Sonntag detected an increasingly bitter note in Gerhardt's comments, calling them "reminiscent of the end of the FDP-Social Democrat coalition" in the early 1980s.

While Kohl's own Christian Democrats have been reluctant to risk the government's slim 10-seat majority, the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) of Finance Minister Theo Waigel has been ready to go into battle.
Gerhardt accused Waigel of papering over cracks in the budget and pretending the situation was less dramatic than it was.
"I'm fed up with the fact that every week we have to discuss the budget on the basis of new figures," he said.
Waigel has already accused the FDP of failing to do its share in finding ways to fill the gap.

His CSU general-secretary Bernd Protzner crowed over the FDP's retreat on tax, telling Sunday's weekly Welt am Sonntag: "The FDP had got its way and now, faced with the real facts, has had to climb down."
He said the two-point cut in the 7.5 percent "solidarity surcharge" on income tax, now postponed from July 1997, might not even take place six months later, as the FDP insists.
"That hasn't been decided yet," Protzner said.
FDP economics spokesman Otto Lambsdorff hit back by accusing the CSU of trying to conceal its own internal problems with the tax row.
"For some time we have found that the CSU's (internal rivalries) are being carried out to the detriment of cooperation in the coalition," he told Sunday's Tagesspiegel.

Even without the cut in the solidarity surcharge, Waigel needs to produce another three billion marks ($1.97 billion) to four billion marks in savings before the parliamentary budget committee meets on November 14 to make up the latest shortfalls in the 1997 budget.
The FDP has secured a commitment that there will be no increase in fuel tax, but is pressing to ensure that all the remaining shortfall is made up from budget savings.

Waigel has suggested that capital spending-intensive ministries such as defence, transport and research cannot be asked to make still bigger cuts than were imposed in an austerity round several months ago.
But Lambsdorff was adamant the coalition partners had agreed no one could automatically be exempted from more spending cuts.
"When it's a question of having to save billions, it would be utterly wrong to exempt certain areas from the outset," he said. ($1=1.5250 Mark)
